stories.title: Why AI is not yet showing up in productivity data
points: Zerodha Varsity revisits Robert Solow's 1987 quip that computers were visible everywhere except the productivity statistics; US trend labour productivity growth had slid from 3.8% in 1948 to 1.2%.

History shows a lag: factories gained from electricity only after redesigning around individual motors, lifting manufacturing productivity 5.3% a year in the 1920s. Computers paid off in the late 1990s.
AI forecasts diverge: Daron Acemoglu sees under 1% over a decade, assuming about 5% of tasks shift to AI; Goldman Sachs sees about 1.5 points a year, assuming about 25%.
stories.why: Firms bolting chatbots onto old workflows may be repeating factory owners who swapped one steam engine for one big motor; the payoff depends on redesigning the work itself.
stories.other: The J-curve is a hypothesis, not a promise: if the gains never arrive, today's AI spending looks less like early investment and more like overbuilding.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on why AI has not yet lifted productivity: Acemoglu estimates under 1% over 10 years, Goldman Sachs about 1.5 points a year, and electricity's gains came only after factory redesign.
stories.emailTeaser: Electricity took nearly four decades to pay off. AI's clock is running.
stories.cite: Zerodha Varsity wrote on 2 November 2026 that Daron Acemoglu estimates AI's total productivity boost at under 1% over 10 years.

stories.title: India's ageing shift needs a three-track policy reset
points: A howindialives.com piece in Mint says India is still young, but the share of people aged 60 and over, about 10% now, is projected to double in two decades, while the working-age share peaks around 2031.
Fertility in eight states has slipped below the level demographers link to a low-fertility trap, yet family planning still rewards sterilisation. It urges rebalancing, not control.
For older adults it proposes trained, better-paid caregivers, Keralam-style day-care centres and ASHA workers retrained for geriatric care; for workers, cities young families want to live in.
stories.why: India's growth story leans on its working-age bulge; building care systems and family-friendly cities now is cheaper than scrambling after that bulge peaks.
stories.other: Pro-natal incentives have done little in rich countries, and with the workforce still growing, scarce public money may do more for jobs today than for births tomorrow.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on India's demographic reset: the 60-plus share, about 10% today, is projected to double in two decades, prompting three policy tracks for fertility, the elderly and workers.
stories.emailTeaser: The elderly share is set to double; policy still fears a boom.

stories.title: India's three trade-offs: fuel prices, rates and foreign money
points: Deepa Vasudevan writes in Mint that the West Asia war has sharpened three balances for India: cheap fuel versus market prices, savers versus borrowers, and foreign money versus fiscal health.
Holding pump prices down only delays inflation. With wholesale inflation at 11.4%, either the RBI keeps raising rates or retail fuel prices rise, possibly after Diwali.
Net capital inflows that averaged $50bn a year until 2023-24 have nearly dried up. Tax breaks for foreign investors might help, but would cost revenue as the deficit risks overshooting.
stories.why: Every lever helps one group and hurts another; the real danger is pulling several at once, such as cutting taxes for foreign investors just as subsidies and borrowing climb.
stories.other: These trade-offs can ease on their own: if crude prices fall, fuel, inflation and rate pressures soften together and the hardest choices fade.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on India's three policy trade-offs over fuel, interest rates and foreign capital, with wholesale inflation at 11.4%.
stories.emailTeaser: Fuel, rates and the rupee pull in different directions.

stories.title: Elliott warns of FOGO as bear-market alarm bells ring
points: In an October investor letter seen by the WSJ, Paul Singer's Elliott likens today's debt-fuelled, hype-driven market to the Roaring '20s and says almost every bear-market warning is flashing.
It lists US deficits, sticky inflation, private credit, AI hype and circular AI deals, plus gambling-like trading, and warns the mood could flip from FOMO to fear of getting obliterated.
Elliott itself has lagged, gaining under 2% in the first nine months of 2026 against nearly 13% for the S&P 500, and is keeping capital ready for forced sellers.
stories.why: When a famously cautious fund trails the market, its warning also defends its own positioning; readers should weigh the list of risks more than the timing.
stories.other: Elliott's letters are known for gloom, and frothy markets can run for years; being early on a crash can cost nearly as much as missing it.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on Elliott's warning of a bear market: it gained under 2% in the first nine months of 2026 against nearly 13% for the S&P 500, and lists deficits, private credit and AI hype as risks.
stories.emailTeaser: A cautious fund says nearly every bear-market alarm is ringing.

stories.title: What caused the Binance hack? Eswar Prasad blames crypto's middlemen
points: Cornell economist Eswar Prasad argues the $6.3bn hack of Binance shows how crypto's promise of decentralisation has been undercut by big centralised exchanges.
The blockchains were not breached, he says; the weak points lie in the ecosystem around them, from exchanges to oracle software, plus human error such as an apparently compromised laptop.
He warns AI is helping hackers, including from North Korea, find subtle flaws, and urges regulators to stop a loss of trust spilling into mainstream finance.
stories.why: Investors park coins on exchanges for convenience, recreating the single point of failure crypto was built to remove; that trade-off now carries a record price tag.
stories.other: Banks get hacked too, and exchanges offer customers the reassurance that losses can be fixed, something a pure self-custody world would not.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on the $6.3bn Binance hack: the blockchain held, but exchanges, a compromised laptop and AI-assisted hackers were the weak points, argues Eswar Prasad.
stories.emailHead: One laptop, a record crypto heist
stories.emailTeaser: Prasad says exchanges, not blockchains, are crypto's weak spot.

stories.title: UK workers less willing to go the extra mile, survey shows
points: A Resolution Foundation analysis of the British Social Attitudes Survey finds UK workers more disengaged than a decade ago, with job satisfaction the gloomiest in the survey's history.
The share willing to work harder than required fell from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025; managers and professionals pulled back most, and men cooled more than women.
The think tank points to post-pandemic priorities, remote work, heavier demands and fewer chances to advance, and says the shift could help explain weak UK productivity.
stories.why: If effort, not just hours or capital, is slipping, part of Britain's productivity problem lies in management and job design, which investment alone won't fix.
stories.other: The survey measures stated willingness, not output; staff who already feel always on may say they do less extra while working just as hard.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer on UK quiet quitting: 55% of workers were willing to work harder than required in 2025, down from 69% in 2015, with managers and men pulling back most.
stories.emailHead: Britain stops going the extra mile
stories.emailTeaser: Fewer staff will do more than required; productivity may pay.

takeaway.line: From crypto vaults to ageing states, systems tend to fail at their weakest point, not their flashiest one.
